lead: A random process is a family of random waveforms indexed by time: one outcome gives one waveform, and the whole family is the ensemble. Noise, speech and fading are modelled this way. For a wide-sense stationary process the mean is constant and the autocorrelation depends only on the time gap τ; its Fourier transform, the power spectral density (PSD), shows how the average power is spread over frequency, and a filter multiplies it by |H(f)|².
prereq: You need: Probability and random variables review (mean, variance, joint variables) and the Fourier pairs in Fourier transform review and band-pass signals.

blocks.text: A random process X(t) assigns a random variable to every time t. Fix one outcome and you get a sample function x(t), one realization. Fix a time t and you get a random variable X(t). The set of all sample functions is the ensemble.

The mean is μX(t) = E[X(t)], an average across the ensemble at one instant. The autocorrelation compares the process at two instants: RX(t1, t2) = E[X(t1)X(t2)]. For a voltage across 1 Ω its unit is watts (strictly V²). The autocovariance removes the mean: CX(t1, t2) = RX(t1, t2) − μX(t1)μX(t2), and CX(t, t) is the variance at time t.

For two processes the cross-correlation is RXY(t1, t2) = E[X(t1)Y(t2)]. It measures how one signal follows the other at a delay. RXY and RYX are different functions, but for jointly stationary processes they are time-reversed copies: RXY(τ) = RYX(−τ).

A process is strict-sense stationary when every joint distribution depends only on time differences, not on absolute time. That is hard to check, so communication work uses wide-sense stationarity (WSS): the mean is a constant μX, and the autocorrelation depends only on the gap τ.

blocks.where: τ is the time gap in seconds; the same R<sub>X</sub>(τ) results whatever t is chosen.

items: R<sub>X</sub>(0) = E[X²(t)], the average power. The variance is R<sub>X</sub>(0) − μ<sub>X</sub>².
R<sub>X</sub>(−τ) = R<sub>X</sub>(τ): the autocorrelation of a real process is even.
|R<sub>X</sub>(τ)| ≤ R<sub>X</sub>(0): no delay gives more correlation than zero delay.
A periodic component in X(t) gives a periodic component in R<sub>X</sub>(τ).

blocks.text: A strict-sense stationary process is also WSS; the reverse holds only for Gaussian processes. A process is ergodic when time averages of one long sample function equal the ensemble averages, so μX and RX(τ) can be measured from a single recording. WSS does not imply ergodic: a random DC level (each sample function is a different constant) is WSS, yet one recording never shows the ensemble mean.

sections.h3: PSD, the Wiener–Khinchin theorem and filtering

blocks.text: A stationary process lasts for ever with finite average power, so each sample function has infinite energy and no ordinary Fourier transform. Its power is described instead by the power spectral density SX(f) in W/Hz. The Wiener–Khinchin theorem (also spelt Wiener–Khinchine; some syllabi call SX the power density spectrum) says that RX(τ) and SX(f) are a Fourier pair:

blocks.where: the integral runs over all τ; S<sub>X</sub>(f) is the two-sided PSD; the inverse is R<sub>X</sub>(τ) = ∫ S<sub>X</sub>(f) e<sup>j2πfτ</sup> df.

blocks.text: Setting τ = 0 in the inverse gives the power: P = R<sub>X</sub>(0) = ∫ S<sub>X</sub>(f) df over all f. For a real process S<sub>X</sub>(f) is real, never negative and even. A one-sided PSD folds the negative frequencies onto the positive ones, so it is twice the two-sided value for f > 0 and is integrated from 0 only.
Pass a WSS process X(t) through an LTI filter H(f). The output Y(t) is WSS, its mean is μ<sub>Y</sub> = H(0)μ<sub>X</sub>, and

blocks.where: |H(f)|² is the power gain at frequency f; the output power is P<sub>Y</sub> = ∫ S<sub>Y</sub>(f) df = R<sub>Y</sub>(0).

blocks.text: For example, white noise of two-sided PSD N<sub>0</sub>/2 through an ideal low-pass filter (gain 1 for |f| ≤ B) gives P<sub>Y</sub> = (N<sub>0</sub>/2)(2B) = N<sub>0</sub>B, and its autocorrelation is the inverse transform of a rectangle: R<sub>Y</sub>(τ) = N<sub>0</sub>B sinc(2Bτ), which first crosses zero at τ = 1/(2B). Samples of this noise taken 1/(2B) apart are uncorrelated.

examples.question: White noise of two-sided PSD N<sub>0</sub>/2 = 1×10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz passes through an ideal low-pass filter of bandwidth B = 10 kHz and unit gain. Find the output PSD, the output power, the output autocorrelation R<sub>Y</sub>(τ) and its first zero.
steps: Input PSD: S<sub>X</sub>(f) = 1×10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz at every f. Power gain |H(f)|² = 1 for |f| ≤ 10 kHz and 0 outside.
Output PSD: S<sub>Y</sub>(f) = 1×10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz for |f| ≤ 10 kHz, 0 outside: a rectangle 20 kHz wide.
Output power = area of the rectangle = (1×10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz)(2 × 10<sup>4</sup> Hz) = 0.02 W = 20 mW. Check: N<sub>0</sub>B = (2×10<sup>−6</sup>)(10<sup>4</sup>) = 0.02 W.
Inverse transform of the rectangle (height S = 10<sup>−6</sup>, half-width B): R<sub>Y</sub>(τ) = 2SB sinc(2Bτ) = 0.02 sinc(2×10<sup>4</sup>τ) W.
R<sub>Y</sub>(0) = 20 mW, the power found in step 3. The first zero is at 2Bτ = 1, τ = 1/(2B) = 50 µs; further zeros at 100 µs, 150 µs and so on.
examples.answer: S<sub>Y</sub>(f) = 1×10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz for |f| ≤ 10 kHz; P<sub>Y</sub> = 20 mW; R<sub>Y</sub>(τ) = 20 mW × sinc(2×10<sup>4</sup>τ), first zero at τ = 50 µs.

examples.question: X(t) = A cos(2πf<sub>0</sub>t + Θ) with A = 2 V, f<sub>0</sub> = 1 kHz and Θ uniform on [0, 2π). Show that X is WSS, find R<sub>X</sub>(τ), its values at τ = 0, 0.25 ms and 0.5 ms, and S<sub>X</sub>(f).
steps: Mean: E[X(t)] = A ∫ cos(2πf<sub>0</sub>t + θ)(1/2π) dθ over one full cycle = 0, for every t.
Product: X(t + τ)X(t) = (A²/2)[cos(2πf<sub>0</sub>τ) + cos(4πf<sub>0</sub>t + 2πf<sub>0</sub>τ + 2Θ)]. The second term averages to zero over Θ.
So R<sub>X</sub>(τ) = (A²/2) cos(2πf<sub>0</sub>τ) = 2 cos(2π × 10³ τ) W, which depends only on τ: with the constant mean, X is WSS.
R<sub>X</sub>(0) = 2 W, the power of a 2 V sinusoid (A²/2). At τ = 0.25 ms the angle is 90°, so R = 0. At τ = 0.5 ms it is 180°, so R = −2 W: samples half a period apart are exact opposites.
Transform with the cosine pair: S<sub>X</sub>(f) = (A²/4)[δ(f − f<sub>0</sub>) + δ(f + f<sub>0</sub>)] = 1 W at ±1 kHz, two impulses whose areas add to 2 W.
examples.answer: μ<sub>X</sub> = 0 and R<sub>X</sub>(τ) = 2 cos(2π×10³τ) W, so X is WSS; R = 2 W, 0 and −2 W at τ = 0, 0.25 ms and 0.5 ms; S<sub>X</sub>(f) = 1 W·δ(f ∓ 1 kHz).

traps: R<sub>X</sub>(0) is the average power E[X²], not the variance. The variance is R<sub>X</sub>(0) − μ<sub>X</sub>²; they are equal only for a zero-mean process.
A two-sided PSD is integrated from −∞ to ∞; a one-sided PSD is twice as tall and integrated from 0. Mixing the two halves or doubles the answer.
The output PSD uses |H(f)|², not H(f). A filter with voltage gain 2 has power gain 4.
The autocorrelation of band-limited white noise is N<sub>0</sub>B sinc(2Bτ): its first zero is at 1/(2B), not 1/B.
Do not write S<sub>X</sub>(f) as |X(f)|² of one sample function. The PSD is the transform of the autocorrelation, an ensemble average.

quiz.a: A process whose mean is constant and whose autocorrelation E[X(t + τ)X(t)] depends only on the gap τ, not on t.

quiz.q: Why is S<sub>X</sub>(f) real, non-negative and even for a real WSS process?
quiz.a: R<sub>X</sub>(τ) is real and even, so its transform is real and even. S<sub>X</sub>(f) is a power density: the power passed by any narrow filter, S<sub>X</sub>(f)Δf, cannot be negative.

quiz.q: White noise with N<sub>0</sub>/2 = 2×10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz passes an ideal low-pass filter of bandwidth 5 kHz. Find the output power.
A WSS process has mean 2 V and R<sub>X</sub>(0) = 13 W (1 Ω). Find its average power, its variance and its AC power.
quiz.a: Average power R<sub>X</sub>(0) = 13 W. Variance = 13 − 2² = 9 V², so the AC (fluctuating) power is 9 W in 1 Ω and the DC power 4 W.

quiz.q: White noise with N<sub>0</sub>/2 = 1×10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz drives an RC low-pass filter H(f) = 1/(1 + jf/f<sub>0</sub>) with f<sub>0</sub> = 1 kHz. Find the output PSD and output power.
quiz.a: S<sub>Y</sub>(f) = 10<sup>−6</sup>/(1 + (f/f<sub>0</sub>)²) W/Hz. P<sub>Y</sub> = 10<sup>−6</sup> ∫ df/(1 + (f/f<sub>0</sub>)²) = 10<sup>−6</sup> × πf<sub>0</sub> = 3.14 mW, the same as an ideal filter of width (π/2)f<sub>0</sub> = 1.571 kHz.

quiz.q: Explain why a random DC level is WSS but not ergodic in the mean.
quiz.a: Each sample function is a constant c drawn at random. The mean E[c] and R<sub>X</sub>(τ) = E[c²] do not depend on t, so it is WSS. But the time average of one sample function is its own c, which differs from E[c]; so time and ensemble means disagree.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice a PSD is estimated from finite records by Welch's method, which averages the spectra of overlapping segments. Cyclostationary processes, whose statistics repeat with a period, model digitally modulated signals. Search for Welch PSD estimation and cyclostationarity.

figure.caption: Worked example 1: white noise through the 10 kHz low-pass filter. The output PSD is a 1 µW/Hz rectangle of area 20 mW; its transform, R<sub>Y</sub>(τ) = 20 mW × sinc(2×10<sup>4</sup>τ), peaks at the power and is zero every 50 µs.

spec.aria: Left, a rectangular power spectral density of height 1 microwatt per hertz between minus and plus 10 kilohertz. Right, a sinc-shaped autocorrelation peaking at 20 milliwatts with zeros every 50 microseconds.
